title: The Real Risk of Using Bilingual Staff as Interpreters in Healthcare
summary: Learn when bilingual staff can interpret in healthcare, why bilingual fluency differs from medical interpreter skill, and how hospitals can reduce ad hoc staff interpretation.
body_markdown:
###


They can when the organization has assessed them for the interpreter role and they have the skills needed to interpret accurately and impartially. Speaking two languages by itself does not prove interpreter competence.


###


A bilingual clinician can provide their own care directly in another language. An interpreter carries messages between a patient and another clinician. Those roles use different skills.


###


Current HHS guidance warns covered entities against relying on unqualified staff for language assistance. HHS also states that self-identified proficiency in another language alone is insufficient to show that someone is qualified to interpret.


###


The risks include omissions, role conflict, unclear boundaries, workflow disruption, privacy concerns, and using language skills that were never assessed for medical interpreting.


###


Give staff a professional interpretation option that starts quickly, clearly define who is approved for in-language care or staff interpreting, and track where informal bilingual interpretation is still occurring.
